Abstract:
Abstract In this study, a machine-learning approach based on Gaussian process regression was developed to identify the optimized processing window for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Using this method, we found a new and much larger optimized LPBF processing window than was known before for manufacturing fully dense AlSi10Mg samples (i.e., relative density ≥ 99%). The newly determined optimized processing parameters (e.g., laser power and scan speed) made it possible to achieve previously unattainable combinations of high strength and ductility. The results showed that although the AlSi10Mg specimens exhibited similar Al-Si eutectic microstructures (e.g., cell structures in fine and coarse grains), they displayed large difference in their mechanical properties including hardness (118 - 137 HV 10), ultimate tensile strength (297 - 389 MPa), elongation to failure (6.3 - 10.3%), and fracture toughness (9.9 - 12.7 kJ/m2). The underlying reason was attributed to the subtle microstructural differences that were further revealed using two newly defined morphology indices (i.e., dimensional-scale index Id and shape index Is) based on several key microstructural features obtained from scanning electron microscopy images. It was found that in addition to grain structure, the sub-grain cell size and cell boundary morphology of the LPBF fabricated AlSi10Mg also strongly affected the mechanical properties of the material. The method established in this study can be readily applied to the LPBF process optimization and mechanical properties manipulation of other widely used metals and alloys or newly designed materials.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) enables controlled gyroid lattices, but mapping both process and design to performance remains challenging when datasets are small and interactions are non-linear. In this study, data-driven models that link energy density and lattice geometry to Young’s modulus and yield strength were established for sheet and network gyroid architectures. To stabilise small-data learning, stacked-autoencoder pre-training was benchmarked against greedy layer-wise pre-training. Compression characterisation data at under-represented energy-density conditions were added to fill data gaps and validate predictions. The models support property-driven design in which given modulus and yield strength targets inform a method that returns feasible combinations of laser powder bed fusion settings and gyroid density and size. Pre-trained models reduced error and captured the relationship between stiffness and density and between strength and density, with yield strength prediction errors of 3.51% for sheet architectures and 8.76% for network architectures. Young’s modulus showed a higher variability that is consistent with sensitivities in LPBF such as surface roughness and thin walls. This work contributes an artificial intelligence method for manufacturing datasets using stacked autoencoder pre-training with fine-tuning, and an inverse-design workflow that maps energy density and gyroid geometry to Young’s modulus and yield strength in titanium lattices.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Data-driven methods are transforming materials design by accelerating the discovery of new compounds and the optimization of existing systems. However, the progress of such approaches is often constrained by the scarcity of high-fidelity data from experiments and advanced simulations. Multi-fidelity (MF) learning has emerged as a powerful strategy to address this challenge by integrating information from diverse data sources that vary in accuracy and cost. In this review, we provide a systematic overview of the major methodologies for MF learning, including statistical and parametric models, machine learning models with fidelity features, correction-based models such as co-kriging, deep learning frameworks, and active learning frameworks. We discuss the strengths, limitations, and typical applications of each method in materials science, with illustrative examples spanning electronic structure modeling, alloy design, and interatomic potential development. Cross-cutting issues are also examined, including the bias-variance trade-off, data requirements for nested vs. non-nested designs, and computational scalability. Finally, we highlight outstanding challenges and outline emerging opportunities, such as physics-informed and generative MF models, standardized datasets, and integration with autonomous laboratories. Together, these perspectives define a roadmap for advancing MF learning as a core enabler of next-generation materials discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We present a multi‐fidelity black‐box optimization approach for integrated design and control (IDC) of constrained nonlinear systems in the presence of uncertainty. The IDC framework is becoming increasingly important for the systematic design of next‐generation (flexible) manufacturing and energy systems. However, identifying optimal solutions to realistic IDC problems is intractable when (i) the dynamics occur on much shorter timescales than the system lifetime, (ii) the uncertainties are described by continuous random variables with high variance, and (iii) operational decisions involve a mixture of discrete and continuous variables. Instead of aggressively simplifying the problem to improve tractability, we develop a simulation‐based optimization procedure using high‐quality decision rules that map information that can be measured online to optimal control actions. In particular, we rely on the Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that has been shown to perform very well on noisy and expensive‐to‐evaluate objective functions. We also discuss how BO can be extended to take advantage of computationally cheaper low‐fidelity approximations to the high‐fidelity IDC cost function. Three major low‐fidelity approximation strategies are described in this work, which are related to the simplification of the system simulator, decision rule solution method, and time grid. Lastly, we demonstrate the advantages of multi‐fidelity BO on the design of a solar‐powered building heating/cooling system (with battery and grid support) under uncertain weather and demand conditions with hourly variation over a year‐long planning horizon.

Abstract:
Resided at the intersection of multi-fidelity optimization (MFO) and Bayesian optimization (BO), MF BO has found a niche in solving expensive engineering design optimization problems, thanks to its advantages in incorporating physical and mathematical understandings of the problems, saving resources, addressing exploitation-exploration trade-off, considering uncertainty, and processing parallel computing. The increasing number of works dedicated to MF BO suggests the need for a comprehensive review of this advanced optimization technique. In this paper, we survey recent developments of two essential ingredients of MF BO: Gaussian process (GP) based MF surrogates and acquisition functions. We first categorize the existing MF modeling methods and MFO strategies to locate MF BO in a large family of surrogate-based optimization and MFO algorithms. We then exploit the common properties shared between the methods from each ingredient of MF BO to describe important GP-based MF surrogate models and review various acquisition functions. By doing so, we expect to provide a structured understanding of MF BO. Finally, we attempt to reveal important aspects that require further research for applications of MF BO in solving intricate yet important design optimization problems, including constrained optimization, high-dimensional optimization, optimization under uncertainty, and multi-objective optimization.

Abstract:
Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sequential optimization strategy that is increasingly employed in a wide range of areas including materials design. In real world applications, acquiring high-fidelity (HF) data through physical experiments or HF simulations is the major cost component of BO. To alleviate this bottleneck, multi-fidelity (MF) methods are used to forgo the sole reliance on the expensive HF data and reduce the sampling costs by querying inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) sources whose data are correlated with HF samples. However, existing multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) methods operate under the following two assumptions that rarely hold in practical applications: (1) LF sources provide data that are well correlated with the HF data on a global scale, and (2) a single random process can model the noise in the fused data. These assumptions dramatically reduce the performance of MFBO when LF sources are only locally correlated with the HF source or when the noise variance varies across the data sources. In this paper, we dispense with these incorrect assumptions by proposing an MF emulation method that (1) learns a noise model for each data source, and (2) enables MFBO to leverage highly biased LF sources which are only locally correlated with the HF source. We illustrate the performance of our method through analytical examples and engineering problems on materials design.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Temperature and humidity calibration chambers, which provide controlled environments for instrument testing and validation, are widely applied in the aerospace and biomedicine fields. However, traditional fixed calibration points fail to adapt to complex operational requirements and exhibit problems including a limited coverage range and low efficiency. To address these challenges, this study develops a Gaussian Process-based Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization (GP-MFBO) framework for optimal selection of temperature and humidity calibration points. The framework integrates the following three key components: (1) a three-layer progressive multi-fidelity modeling system comprising physical analytical models, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) numerical simulations, and experimental verification; (2) a systematic uncertainty quantification system covering model uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, and observation uncertainty; and (3) an adaptive acquisition function that balances uncertainty penalty mechanisms and multi-fidelity information gain evaluation. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GP-MFBO method achieves optimal calibration point combinations with a temperature uniformity score of 0.149 and humidity uniformity score of 2.38, approaching theoretical optimal solutions within 4.5% and 3.6%, respectively. Compared to standard Gaussian process, Co-Kriging, two-stage optimization, polynomial regression, and traditional single-fidelity methods, GP-MFBO achieves uniformity score improvements of up to 81.7% and 76.3% for temperature and humidity, respectively. The prediction confidence interval coverage reaches 94.2%, outperforming all comparative methods. This research provides a rigorous theoretical foundation and technical solution for the scientific design and reliable operation of large-space temperature and humidity calibration systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Process optimization for Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell culture remains a challenge in biopharmaceutical development because multiple interacting parameters jointly influence productivity and product quality attributes. Traditional design-of-experiments (DoE) methods, while systematic, become impractically expensive when extended across multiple parameters and clones. To address this challenge, we developed a multi-objective Bayesian Optimization (BO) framework that identifies optimal process conditions efficiently in grouped recommendations, which is well suited for experimental workflows in bioprocess development. The model integrates continuous variables such as pH, DO, temperature, and feed rate with categorical identifiers to enable knowledge transfer across clones and scales, optimizing titer, glycan profile, and charge variants. We validated the framework through in-silico benchmarks on analytic functions, retrospective cross-validation on historical CHO datasets, and forward experimental validation in small-scale bioreactors. Across these tests, our algorithm consistently outperformed Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) and Random Search baselines, achieving superior performance under a limited experimental budget. The framework improved titer by up to 37% under single-objective optimization. In the multi-objective setting, it increased titer by 25% while simultaneously reducing overall glycan-profile error by a factor of seven, demonstrating the ability to optimize multiple biologically coupled objectives simultaneously. Through comprehensive in-silico and experimental validation, this study establishes a framework that enables adaptive, AI-guided process development and improves decision-making across multiple objectives, clones, and scales while minimizing experimental runs in process development and optimization workflows.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Online experiments in internet systems, also known as A/B tests, are used for a wide range of system tuning problems, such as optimizing recommender system ranking policies and learning adaptive streaming controllers. Decision-makers generally wish to optimize for long-term treatment effects of the system changes, which often requires running experiments for a long time as short-term measurements can be misleading due to non-stationarity in treatment effects over time. The sequential experimentation strategies---which typically involve several iterations---can be prohibitively long in such cases. We describe a novel approach that combines fast experiments (e.g., biased experiments run only for a few hours or days) and/or offline proxies (e.g., off-policy evaluation) with long-running, slow experiments to perform sequential, Bayesian optimization over large action spaces in a short amount of time.

Abstract:
Designing neural architectures requires immense manual efforts. This has promoted the development of neural architecture search (NAS) to automate the design. While previous NAS methods achieve promising results but run slowly, zero-cost proxies run extremely fast but are less promising. Therefore, it’s of great potential to accelerate NAS via those zero-cost proxies. The existing method has two limitations, which are unforeseeable reliability and one-shot usage. To address the limitations, we present ProxyBO, an efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that utilizes the zero-cost proxies to accelerate neural architecture search. We apply the generalization ability measurement to estimate the fitness of proxies on the task during each iteration and design a novel acquisition function to combine BO with zero-cost proxies based on their dynamic influence. Extensive empirical studies show that ProxyBO consistently outperforms competitive baselines on five tasks from three public benchmarks. Concretely, ProxyBO achieves up to 5.41× and 3.86× speedups over the state-of-the-art approaches REA and BRP-NAS.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The opto-mechanical automated manufacturing process, characterized by stringent process constraints, dynamic disturbances, and conflicting optimization objectives, presents significant control challenges for traditional scheduling and control approaches. We formulate the scheduling problem within a closed-loop control paradigm and propose a novel bi-level intelligent control framework integrating Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Bayesian Optimization (BO). The core of our approach is a bi-level intelligent control framework. An inner DRL agent acts as an adaptive controller, generating control actions (scheduling decisions) by perceiving the system state and learning a near-optimal policy through a carefully designed reward function, while an outer BO loop automatically tunes the DRL’s hyperparameters and reward weights for superior performance. This synergistic BO-DRL mechanism facilitates intelligent and adaptive decision-making. The proposed method is extensively evaluated against standard meta-heuristics, including Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), on a complex 20-jobs × 20-machines flexible job shop scheduling benchmark specific to opto-mechanical automated manufacturing. The experimental results demonstrate that our BO-DRL algorithm significantly outperforms these benchmarks, achieving reductions in makespan of 13.37% and 25.51% compared to GA and PSO, respectively, alongside higher machine utilization and better on-time delivery. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits enhanced convergence speed, superior robustness under dynamic disruptions (e.g., machine failures, urgent orders), and excellent scalability to larger problem instances. This study confirms that integrating DRL’s perceptual decision-making capability with BO’s efficient parameter optimization yields a powerful and effective solution for intelligent scheduling in high-precision manufacturing environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Offline optimization is a fundamental challenge in science and engineering, where the goal is to optimize black-box functions using only offline datasets. This setting is particularly relevant when querying the objective function is prohibitively expensive or infeasible, with applications spanning protein engineering, material discovery, neural architecture search, and beyond. The main difficulty lies in accurately estimating the objective landscape beyond the available data, where extrapolations are fraught with significant epistemic uncertainty. This uncertainty can lead to objective hacking(reward hacking), exploiting model inaccuracies in unseen regions, or other spurious optimizations that yield misleadingly high performance estimates outside the training distribution. Recent advances in model-based optimization(MBO) have harnessed the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks to develop offline-specific surrogate and generative models. Trained with carefully designed strategies, these models are more robust against out-of-distribution issues, facilitating the discovery of improved designs. Despite its growing impact in accelerating scientific discovery, the field lacks a comprehensive review. To bridge this gap, we present the first thorough review of offline MBO. We begin by formalizing the problem for both single-objective and multi-objective settings and by reviewing recent benchmarks and evaluation metrics. We then categorize existing approaches into two key areas: surrogate modeling, which emphasizes accurate function approximation in out-of-distribution regions, and generative modeling, which explores high-dimensional design spaces to identify high-performing designs. Finally, we examine the key challenges and propose promising directions for advancement in this rapidly evolving field including safe control of superintelligent systems.

Abstract:
Particle accelerators require constant tuning during operation to meet beam quality, total charge and particle energy requirements for use in a wide variety of physics, chemistry and biology experiments. Maximizing the performance of an accelerator facility often necessitates multi-objective optimization, where operators must balance trade-offs between multiple objectives simultaneously, often using limited, temporally expensive beam observations. Usually, accelerator optimization problems are solved offline, prior to actual operation, with advanced beamline simulations and parallelized optimization methods (NSGA-II, Swarm Optimization). Unfortunately, it is not feasible to use these methods for online multi-objective optimization, since beam measurements can only be done in a serial fashion, and these optimization methods require a large number of measurements to converge to a useful solution.Here, we introduce a multi-objective Bayesian optimization scheme, which finds the full Pareto front of an accelerator optimization problem efficiently in a serialized manner and is thus a critical step towards practical online multi-objective optimization in accelerators.This method uses a set of Gaussian process surrogate models, along with a multi-objective acquisition function, which reduces the number of observations needed to converge by at least an order of magnitude over current methods.We demonstrate how this method can be modified to specifically solve optimization challenges posed by the tuning of accelerators.This includes the addition of optimization constraints, objective preferences and costs related to changing accelerator parameters.

Abstract:
This paper introduces a modular framework for Mixed-variable and Combinatorial Bayesian Optimization (MCBO) to address the lack of systematic benchmarking and standardized evaluation in the field. Current MCBO papers often introduce non-diverse or non-standard benchmarks to evaluate their methods, impeding the proper assessment of different MCBO primitives and their combinations. Additionally, papers introducing a solution for a single MCBO primitive often omit benchmarking against baselines that utilize the same methods for the remaining primitives. This omission is primarily due to the significant implementation overhead involved, resulting in a lack of controlled assessments and an inability to showcase the merits of a contribution effectively. To overcome these challenges, our proposed framework enables an effortless combination of Bayesian Optimization components, and provides a diverse set of synthetic and real-world benchmarking tasks. Leveraging this flexibility, we implement 47 novel MCBO algorithms and benchmark them against seven existing MCBO solvers and five standard black-box optimization algorithms on ten tasks, conducting over 4000 experiments. Our findings reveal a superior combination of MCBO primitives outperforming existing approaches and illustrate the significance of model fit and the use of a trust region. We make our MCBO library available under the MIT license at \url{https://github.com/huawei-noah/HEBO/tree/master/MCBO}.

We consider a sequential assortment selection problem where the user choice is given by a multinomial logit (MNL) choice model whose parameters are unknown. In each period, the learning agent observes a d-dimensional contextual information about the user and the N available items, and offers an assortment of size K to the user, and observes the bandit feedback of the item chosen from the assortment. We propose upper confidence bound based algorithms for this MNL contextual bandit. The first algorithm is a simple and practical method that achieves an O(d√T) regret over T rounds. Next, we propose a second algorithm which achieves a O(√dT) regret. This matches the lower bound for the MNL bandit problem, up to logarithmic terms, and improves on the best-known result by a √d factor. To establish this sharper regret bound, we present a non-asymptotic confidence bound for the maximum likelihood estimator of the MNL model that may be of independent interest as its own theoretical contribution. We then revisit the simpler, significantly more practical, first algorithm and show that a simple variant of the algorithm achieves the optimal regret for a broad class of important applications.

Abstract:
A problem that arises in slice-selective magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radio-frequency (RF) excitation pulse design is abstracted as a novel linear inverse problem with a simultaneous sparsity constraint. Multiple unknown signal vectors are to be determined, where each passes through a different system matrix and the results are added to yield a single observation vector. Abstract:
In order to push the performance on realistic computer vision tasks, the number of classes in modern benchmark datasets has significantly increased in recent years. This increase in the number of classes comes along with increased ambiguity between the class labels, raising the question if top-1 error is the right performance measure. In this paper, we provide an extensive comparison and evaluation of established multiclass methods comparing their top-k performance both from a practical as well as from a theoretical perspective. Moreover, we introduce novel top-k loss functions as modifications of the softmax and the multiclass SVM losses and provide efficient optimization schemes for them. Loeppky, Sacks, and Welch provide empirical and theoretical support for using approximately n = 10d runs in an effective initial computer experiment, where d is the number of input variables. Thus, the 10d rule means allocating about ten simulator evaluations per input dimension—for example, roughly 100 runs for a 10-dimensional input space. The recommendation is presented as a practical rule of thumb rather than a universal sample-size formula, since the required number of runs depends on characteristics of the computer code and the desired prediction accuracy. In their Gaussian-process (GP) framework, two especially relevant characteristics are the total sensitivity of the output to all inputs and how that sensitivity is distributed: a small number of prominent factors versus many weak or impotent factors (effect sparsity). These characteristics determine the GP correlation structure and can substantially affect the sample size needed. The article motivates the rule using simulation evidence and examples, while noting that high dimensionality can create a curse-of-dimensionality problem; conversely, if total sensitivity is spread across many variables, dimensionality may have a more limited effect. Standard Bayesian optimization may begin with random or Latin Hypercube samples, which can make initial progress slow, particularly in combinatorially large spaces, because it lacks domain knowledge and contextual understanding. The proposed BORA framework instead couples an LLM with standard BO and uses contextual, domain-informed hypotheses to suggest promising regions for sampling. Importantly, the LLM is intended to regulate its contribution adaptively, especially when the search becomes trapped in local minima, rather than permanently replacing stochastic exploration. The excerpt reports that context-aware suggestions improved optimization performance in several real-world scientific tasks, including chemical materials design, solar energy, and crop production, but it does not establish whether warm-starting universally helps or hurts. It highlights important risks: expert or literature-based seeds can introduce confirmation bias, overemphasize familiar regions, and cause users or models to overlook promising but underrepresented areas of the search space. Such biased initial data could also steer the surrogate model toward known regions and reduce exploration of novel optima. The stated goal of dynamic commentary and possible user intervention is intended to help detect or correct these effects.

The excerpt does not explicitly describe BoTorch fantasizing, conditioning on pending evaluations, or the distinction between fantasized outcomes and pseudo-observations used as GP priors. It does provide relevant guidance for incorporating heterogeneous information sources and noisier literature data. Different sources can be represented with a source-indexed or multi-information-source surrogate, where the covariance includes both similarity between candidate conditions and covariance between information sources. When sources have systematic discrepancies, the model should represent both correlation and bias rather than treating all observations as interchangeable. The discussion of noise cautions against assuming every observation is equally reliable: a constant-noise GP is a practical baseline, but reliability may vary across process space and input-dependent noise can arise from characterization or synthesis. Noise that is set too low can cause the GP to overfit noisy observations, while noise set too high can oversmooth the response. Thus, literature measurements with greater uncertainty are most relevantly treated as observations with appropriately larger, source-specific or heteroscedastic noise, rather than as exact pseudo-data. The excerpt also notes that related tasks or sources can cause negative transfer when assumed relationships are incorrect, which is relevant when combining literature and current experimental data.

## pqac-00000051

From text 'foumani2023ontheeffects pages 3-5'.

Zahra Zanjani Foumani, Amin Yousefpour, Mehdi Shishehbor, and Ramin Bostanabad. On the effects of heterogeneous errors on multi-fidelity bayesian optimization. ArXiv, Sep 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2309.02771, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2309.02771. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt does not describe BoTorch’s fantasizing procedure, conditioning on pending evaluations, pseudo-observations, or synthetic prior data. It does, however, discuss how data sources with different noise levels should be represented in a Gaussian-process-based multi-fidelity model. Standard MFBO is described as assuming that all sources share the same noise process and unknown noise variance. This is problematic when sources differ substantially—for example, when some are deterministic simulations and others are physical experiments—because the model can overestimate uncertainty for effectively noise-free sources and thereby reduce optimization performance. The proposed MFBOUQ approach instead estimates a separate noise process for each data source, allowing heterogeneous observation noise to be modeled explicitly. It also retains low-fidelity sources even when they are biased relative to the high-fidelity source, rather than discarding them solely because of that bias. In the LMGP formulation, source identity is introduced as a categorical variable; observations from all sources are concatenated and jointly modeled, while the learned latent representation captures relationships among sources. These points support incorporating noisier literature data through source-specific noise modeling and uncertainty calibration, rather than treating such data as equally reliable observations or using them as unqualified synthetic prior information.

## pqac-00000052

From text 'wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 19-21'.

Y. Wakabayashi and T. Otsuka. Bayesian optimization for self-driving materials laboratories: from algorithms to physics-informed workflows. ArXiv, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt does not discuss BoTorch’s fantasizing mechanism, conditioning on pending evaluations, or the distinction between sampled pending outcomes and pseudo-observations used as GP priors. It does provide relevant guidance for handling observations with different reliability. Observation noise can depend on experimental conditions because of changes in characterization quality or synthesis reproducibility. Heteroscedastic Gaussian-process models can represent this input-dependent noise, but sparse single-shot data make it difficult to distinguish genuine changes in the latent materials response from changes in measurement noise. Consequently, noise variation should ideally be constrained using replicate measurements at identical or nearby conditions, uncertainty estimates from spectral fitting, detector statistics, or other metadata. Without such information, a flexible heteroscedastic model may be unstable or poorly calibrated, and a constant-noise model may be safer. This supports assigning higher, explicitly modeled observation noise to less reliable literature measurements rather than treating them as precise pseudo-observations that pull the latent GP mean toward their values. The excerpt also emphasizes that uncertainty estimates must be reliable because they directly control exploration–exploitation decisions in Bayesian optimization.

## pqac-00000053

Additively manufacturable high-strength aluminum alloys with thermally stable microstructures enabled by hybrid machine learning-based design. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2406.17457, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2406.17457. This article has 11 citations.

The excerpt describes an ICME–machine-learning/Bayesian optimization workflow for designing high-strength, LPBF-compatible aluminum alloys. Thermo-Calc-based ICME simulations supplied composition-dependent descriptors, including precipitate fractions, coarsening behavior, solvus temperatures, and printability-related metrics. Bayesian optimization searched composition space while minimizing the coarsening metric and constraining Er and Zr contents to control L12 and Al3Zr precipitates. A neural-network surrogate model was trained using composition as input and coarsening metric as the target; this reduced the number of expensive ICME evaluations needed. The optimized composition had a normalized coarsening metric 3.5 times lower than the benchmark alloy. Scheil solidification simulations were then used to optimize Ni, because a metastable Al23Ni6M4 ternary phase formed during solidification and acted as a reservoir for nanoscale L12 precipitation during aging. Printability constraints were evaluated using crack-susceptibility metrics, and candidate compositions were experimentally screened through induction melting and laser scanning before custom powder was atomized and 3D printed. The selected alloy was crack-free, exhibited 180 HV in the as-built state, and reached 147 HV after aging. This excerpt does not provide optimization details for AlSi10Mg or Scalmalloy specifically.

## pqac-00000054

Additively manufacturable high-strength aluminum alloys with thermally stable microstructures enabled by hybrid machine learning-based design. Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2406.17457, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2406.17457. This article has 11 citations.

The excerpt describes an inverse-design workflow combining CALPHAD-based integrated computational materials engineering (ICME), machine learning, and Bayesian optimization. Alloy composition—particularly the concentrations of five alloying elements—was treated as the design space. CALPHAD/ICME calculations predicted phase formation, solidification behavior, precipitate evolution, coarsening rates, and other microstructural characteristics, while machine-learning models captured nonlinear relationships between composition and the desired outcomes. Bayesian optimization efficiently searched this multidimensional space and selected promising compositions rather than requiring exhaustive experimental trials. The objectives were to promote rapid-solidification formation of submicron metastable ternary phases during LPBF, transform these into nanoscale, thermally stable L12 strengthening precipitates during heat treatment, minimize precipitate coarsening and fast-growing phases, and control the solidification temperature range and time to reduce hot cracking. The approach was demonstrated with an Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni model alloy. Candidate compositions were first screened computationally and then evaluated through arc melting and laser scanning before powder production and LPBF validation. The designed alloy achieved strength comparable to wrought Al7075 without its LPBF cracking problem and was 50% stronger than the strongest benchmark printable Al alloy after aging at 400°C. The excerpt does not describe optimization of AlSi10Mg or Scalmalloy specifically.

The excerpt describes an ICME-plus-machine-learning workflow for designing LPBF aluminum alloys, rather than optimization of a conventional AlSi10Mg or Scalmalloy composition. Thermodynamic and microstructural calculations supplied descriptors such as L12 phase fraction, phase size, coarsening metric, cracking susceptibility (CSC), flow range (FR), and hot-cracking susceptibility (HCS). Elemental mole percentages were used as inputs to surrogate models. Six regressors were compared; a neural-network model best captured the nonlinear relationship between alloy composition and coarsening, reaching approximately 3% normalized prediction error with 40 training compositions. Bayesian optimization was then used for inverse design. A Gaussian-process surrogate, Latin-hypercube sampling, and expected improvement balanced exploration and exploitation while searching composition space. Design objectives included maximizing L12 strengthening phases, minimizing coarsening, and satisfying LPBF printability constraints. Optimizing printability alone favored eutectic phases such as Al3Ni, which improved processability but harmed high-temperature mechanical performance. The selected strategy therefore prioritized low coarsening while constraining Er and Zr to control L12 and Al3Zr formation. The reported optimized alloy achieved about 40% higher L12 fraction and a 3.5-fold reduction in coarsening metric versus the benchmark, while meeting printability requirements. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001) | High | Use about **7 common seed runs** (28%): three baselines, two knowledge-based candidates, and two constrained space-filling augmentations. Move the saved runs into adaptive BO rounds. |
| P2 | Loeppky et al.’s approximately **10d rule** would require roughly 140–150 observations for a 14–15-dimensional continuous composition representation—impossible here. Moreover, that rule concerns accurate GP emulation of deterministic computer codes, not necessarily optimization under a 25-run physical budget. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) | High | Reduce effective dimension before atomization: encode element-set choice categorically, use at most four active additions, exploit CALPHAD descriptors and metallurgy-informed screening, and fit sparse or hierarchical kernels rather than pretending nine runs identify 15 independent length scales. |
| P3 | Expert-, literature-, CALPHAD-, and LLM-selected seeds are likely to cluster around familiar Al–Si–Mg and Al–Mg–Sc–Zr families. Warm starts can improve early performance, but LLAMBO generated less-diverse, correlated points; knowledge-based proposals can reinforce confirmation bias and make the GP overconfident in known regions. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) | High | Limit knowledge-based physical seeds to about two, require distinct strengthening hypotheses and element sets, label provenance, and reserve at least two seeds for deliberately dissimilar coverage points. Compare against a model using only unbiased common seeds. |
| P4 | A scrambled Sobol design in the nominal 15-element simplex is geometrically mismatched to the feasible set. Almost all generic points violate the “at most four additions” rule or occupy irrelevant high-order mixtures; projection or repair can create clustering and destroy Sobol balance. Mixture spaces require simplex-aware designs. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042) | High | Generate a large candidate pool **directly on the union of feasible sparse simplexes**: first sample admissible element subsets, then sample bounded compositions within each selected face. Perform augmentation against all fixed baseline and knowledge-based points. |
| P5 | “At most k non-zero additions” is a combinatorial **NChooseK constraint**, but the plan specifies no metric, subset-allocation rule, or kernel for the resulting disconnected union of simplex faces. Ordinary Euclidean maximin can regard alloys with different element identities as misleadingly close or far. | High | Pre-register a mixed distance combining element-set dissimilarity, such as weighted Jaccard or Hamming distance, with an Aitchison or range-scaled distance within a simplex face. Ensure coverage across several metallurgically admissible element subsets before optimizing continuous concentrations. |
| P6 | Composition-level space filling alone does not initialize every BOFN node well. The print GP needs coverage in powder properties, CALPHAD descriptors, and LPBF parameters; property GPs need coverage in achieved microstructure, density, cracking, and heat-treatment states. BOFN studies commonly begin with complete network observations, while node-specific network designs target each node’s own feasible input domain. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028) | High | Obtain several complete end-to-end seed trajectories, then add cheap node-specific data: exhaustive CALPHAD evaluations, commercial-powder LPBF plates, and hardness measurements. Design LPBF conditions in the **print node’s input space**, conditional on observed powder and descriptor outputs, rather than only in nominal composition space. |
| P7 | The proposed “fantasy modelling” conflates two different operations. Synthetic or literature pseudo-observations alter the fitted model and can bias its posterior; BoTorch `fantasize` instead draws possible outcomes at genuinely pending evaluation locations and conditions temporary posterior models for asynchronous or batch acquisition calculations. | Medium | Rename the pre-campaign exercise a **synthetic digital-twin dry run**. Keep pseudo-data in a separate source or fidelity table and exclude it from the physical-data posterior by default. Use BoTorch fantasies only for pending real evaluations, integrating over multiple posterior samples rather than retaining fantasies as observations. |
| P8 | Pooling literature, database, simulation, and in-house measurements as exchangeable observations ignores systematic source bias and heterogeneous noise, inviting negative transfer and false confidence. Multi-fidelity work shows that source-specific noise and discrepancy matter, especially when simulations and experiments differ. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | High | Add source or fidelity indicators, source-specific bias or discrepancy functions, and inflated heteroscedastic noise based on provenance. Prefer multi-task or multi-fidelity GPs, or RGPE-style source models whose influence can fall as target data accumulate. Never silently replace synthetic values with real ones in the same row. |
| P9 | A fair replay comparison requires every policy to start from the same information state. The current three-way seed allocation embeds agent knowledge only in the proposed policy’s initial dataset, so apparent “AI acceleration” could merely measure a better warm start; sparse real trajectories also make exact counterfactual replay impossible away from observed points. | High | Pre-register one **shared common seed set**, objectives, stopping rules, costs, failure handling, and random seeds for all policies. Report warm-start and sequential-policy effects separately. Use retrospective replay only when a policy selects an observed candidate; otherwise use a clearly labelled cross-validated simulator with uncertainty and avoid causal acceleration claims. |
| P10 | The five 6063 repeat atomizations, benchmark repeats, dosing checks, and baseline alloys are not merely overhead. They inform atomizer noise, composition fidelity, calibration, process transfer, and incumbent performance. Excluding them from GP training wastes scarce information; counting duplicates as independent coverage, however, exaggerates design size. | High | Include compatible runs in node-level likelihoods with explicit alloy, source, and run identifiers. Count a unique baseline composition once for **coverage**, but count all independent runs for **noise estimation**. Use the 6063 repeats primarily to estimate run-level variance and drift, not as five distinct composition seeds. |


*Table: The table identifies ten methodological and benchmarking risks in the proposed LPBF alloy campaign and pairs each with a concrete mitigation. It emphasizes effective dimensionality, sparse-mixture geometry, node-specific BOFN coverage, source uncertainty, and fair policy comparison.*

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then

immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain

you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)

quotes, additional tags, etc.).

so that the artifact is properly contextualized.

<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):

because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We are choosing the seed (initial) experiments for a closed-loop Bayesian optimization (BO) campaign that looks for new aluminium alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). Please give a critical, literature-grounded review of our seeding plan. Act as a sceptical rubber duck: say where the plan is wrong, not only where it is right.

SETTING
- Optimizer: BO over a function network (BOFN; Astudillo and Frazier, 2021) with cost-aware partial evaluations (p-KGFN; Buathong, Frazier and co-authors, 2024). Each node of a directed acyclic graph has its own Gaussian process (GP):
  composition (Al balance, at least 85 at.% Al; additions chosen from Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn; at most about 4 additions per alloy)
  -> CALPHAD/Scheil descriptors (freezing range, hot-cracking index, L1_2 and intermetallic fractions; seconds per evaluation)
  -> ultrasonic atomization of a 250 g charge (outputs: particle size distribution, yield in the 15-63 um LPBF cut, oxygen, composition fidelity by SEM-EDS)
  -> LPBF on a research machine (single tracks, then density cubes; inputs laser power, scan speed, hatch, layer thickness; outputs melt-pool depth and width, relative density, crack density)
  -> Vickers hardness (fast strength screen), sub-size tensile (yield strength, UTS, elongation) and corrosion.
  A mineral-burden objective (import-reliance or supply-risk weighted wt%) is analytic.
- Goal: an alloy stronger than LPBF AlSi10Mg and/or as strong as Scalmalloy (Al-Mg-Sc-Zr) with much less critical-mineral (Sc) content.
- Budget: 36 atomizer runs by late February 2027, 3-4 per week. 5 are fixed-setting repeat runs on a 6063 base (to measure run-to-run noise) and 6 are held back for failed runs, which leaves about 25 runs where we choose what to make. Those 25 currently are: 3 benchmark runs (AlSi10Mg-type, Scalmalloy-type, and a repeat of the first), 2 dosing checks at known Si, 4 CALPHAD-chosen seeds, 4 optimizer rounds of 3 runs, and 2 finalists made twice. Single tracks and small cubes are cheap next to atomization (many compositions and parameter sets fit on one build plate); tensile bars are expensive.

PROPOSED SEEDING PLAN (please critique)
About 9 of the 25 runs as seeds, 3 from each of:
 (1) agent-chosen: compositions proposed from the literature, databases, LLM agents and CALPHAD screening;
 (2) known baselines: AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy and similar commercial or literature alloys;
 (3) space-filling exploration: scrambled Sobol in the design space, possibly made more model-based by discarding Sobol points too close to existing (baseline, agent or literature) experiments, by maximin augmentation, or by maximum-variance / IMSE designs from a GP fitted to the existing data.
In parallel, "fantasy modelling": fill each node with synthetic or literature-derived pseudo-observations so that the whole loop can run before real data exist, then replace them with real data as experiments come in.

QUESTIONS (answer each with evidence and DOIs)
1. Initial design size. What does the literature say about the share of a small BO budget (30-50 evaluations or fewer) to spend on the initial design? For example: Bossek et al. (2020) on initial design strategies for sequential model-based optimization; 2d versus 10d rules; Loeppky, Sacks and Welch (2009) for GP emulators; Ax and BoTorch defaults; self-driving-lab case studies. With about 25 decisions, 4 batch rounds of 3, and a design space that is high-dimensional unless reduced, is 9 seeds too many, too few, or about right? How should repeat and baseline runs that are already planned count toward the initial design?
2. Expert, literature and LLM-chosen seeds versus space-filling. What is the evidence from materials and chemistry BO (e.g., LLAMBO warm-starting, expert-initialised campaigns, transfer learning) on whether knowledge-based seeds help or hurt, on the risk of biasing the surrogate toward known regions, and on how to mix them with space-filling points? What is known about including the incumbent or benchmark alloys as seeds?
3. Space-filling that accounts for existing points. Compare methods for augmenting a design around fixed existing points (maximin augmentation, sequential or nested space-filling, Sobol with an exclusion radius, coverage designs, maximum-entropy / variance / IMSE designs) in constrained mixture (simplex) spaces with sparsity (at most k non-zero additions, NChooseK constraints). Which is most practical and defensible for adding only 3-6 points?
4. Seeding a function network. Each node is its own GP whose inputs are upstream outputs plus node-local parameters. Is there literature on initial designs for networks of GPs, multi-stage or cascade processes, or partial evaluations, e.g., seeding downstream nodes from cheaper sources (commercial powders for the print-parameter node, literature tensile data for the property node, CALPHAD for descriptors)? Should space-filling be done in each node's own input space (that is, in the upstream output or descriptor space) rather than in composition space?
5. Literature and synthetic ("fantasy") data as priors. How should literature or database data and simulation outputs enter the GP without biasing it: multi-task or multi-fidelity GPs with a source indicator, prior-mean functions, inflated or heteroscedastic noise for literature points, transfer learning such as RGPE, power-prior down-weighting? How can pseudo-observations be swapped cleanly for real data? Please also clarify how this differs from BoTorch's "fantasize" (conditioning on sampled outcomes at pending points).
6. Making the seeds count for the paper. We will pre-register an "AI acceleration factor" benchmark against random, expert design-of-experiments and standard BO baselines, and replay the policies on our real data. How should the seed design be chosen so that this comparison is fair and possible with so few experiments?

End with (a) a recommended allocation of the 25 runs (baselines, agent-chosen, space-filling, optimizer rounds, finalists), (b) the recommended space-filling method, and (c) the main pitfalls, as a table, plus a reference list with DOIs.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll start by creating a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about seeding strategies for Bayesian optimization in alloy design.

Abstract:
Abstract This article deals with the sequential design of experiments for (deterministic or stochastic) multi-fidelity numerical simulators, that is, simulators that offer control over the accuracy of simulation of the physical phenomenon or system under study. Accurate simulations usually entail a high computational effort, while coarse simulations are obtained at a lower cost. The cost can be measured, for example, by the run time of the simulator or the financial cost of the computing resources. In this setting, simulation results obtained at several levels of fidelity can be combined in order to estimate quantities of interest (the optimal value of the output, the probability that the output exceeds a given threshold, etc.) in an efficient manner. We propose a new Bayesian sequential strategy called maximal rate of stepwise uncertainty reduction (MR-SUR), that selects additional simulations to be performed by maximizing the ratio between the expected reduction of uncertainty and the cost of simulation. This generic strategy unifies several existing methods, and provides a principled approach to develop new ones. We assess its performance on several examples, including a computationally intensive problem of fire safety analysis where the quantity of interest is the probability of exceeding a tenability threshold during a building fire.

Abstract:
Traditional experimental design methods often face challenges in handling complex aerospace systems due to the high dimensionality and nonlinear behavior of such systems, resulting in nonoptimal experimental designs. To address these challenges, machine learning techniques can be used to further increase the application areas of modern Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (BOED) approaches, enhancing their efficiency and accuracy. The proposed method leverages neural networks as surrogate models to approximate the underlying physical processes, thereby reducing computational costs and allowing for full differentiability. Additionally, the use of reinforcement learning enables the optimization of sequential designs and essential real-time capability. Our framework is validated by optimizing experimental designs that are used for the efficient characterization of turbopumps for liquid propellant rocket engines. The reinforcement learning approach yields superior results in terms of the expected information gain related to a sequence of 15 experiments, exhibiting mean performance increases of 9.07% compared to random designs and 6.47% compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Therefore, the results demonstrate significant improvements in experimental efficiency and accuracy compared to conventional methods. This work provides a robust framework for the application of advanced BOED methods in aerospace testing, with implications for broader engineering applications.

Abstract:
Sequential model-based optimization (SMBO) approaches are algorithms for solving problems that require computationally or otherwise expensive function evaluations. The key design principle of SMBO is a substitution of the true objective function by a surrogate, which is used to propose the point(s) to be evaluated next. SMBO algorithms are intrinsically modular, leaving the user with many important design choices. Significant research efforts go into understanding which settings perform best for which type of problems. Most works, however, focus on the choice of the model, the acquisition function, and the strategy used to optimize the latter. The choice of the initial sampling strategy, however, receives much less attention. Not surprisingly, quite diverging recommendations can be found in the literature. We analyze in this work how the size and the distribution of the initial sample influences the overall quality of the efficient global optimization (EGO) algorithm, a well-known SMBO approach. While, overall, small initial budgets using Halton sampling seem preferable, we also observe that the performance landscape is rather unstructured. We furthermore identify several situations in which EGO performs unfavorably against random sampling. Both observations indicate that an adaptive SMBO design could be beneficial, making SMBO an interesting test-bed for automated algorithm design.

We provide reasons and evidence supporting the informal rule that the number of runs for an effective initial computer experiment should be about 10 times the input dimension. Our arguments quantify two key characteristics of computer codes that affect the sample size required for a desired level of accuracy when approximating the code via a Gaussian process (GP). The first characteristic is the total sensitivity of a code output variable to all input variables; the second corresponds to the way this total sensitivity is distributed across the input variables, specifically the possible presence of a few prominent input factors and many impotent ones (i.e., effect sparsity). Both measures relate directly to the correlation structure in the GP approximation of the code. In this way, the article moves toward a more formal treatment of sample size for a computer experiment. The evidence supporting these arguments stems primarily from a simulation study and via specific codes modeling climate and ligand activation of G-protein.

Abstract:
Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful approach for optimizing complex and expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions. Its importance is underscored in many applications, notably including hyperparameter tuning, but its efficacy depends on efficiently balancing exploration and exploitation. While there has been substantial progress in BO methods, striking this balance remains a delicate process. In this light, we present LLAMBO, a novel approach that integrates the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLM) within BO. At a high level, we frame the BO problem in natural language, enabling LLMs to iteratively propose and evaluate promising solutions conditioned on historical evaluations. More specifically, we explore how combining contextual understanding, few-shot learning proficiency, and domain knowledge of LLMs can improve model-based BO. Our findings illustrate that LLAMBO is effective at zero-shot warmstarting, and enhances surrogate modeling and candidate sampling, especially in the early stages of search when observations are sparse. Abstract:
Many important scientific problems involve multivariate optimization coupled with slow and laborious experimental measurements. These complex, high-dimensional searches can be defined by non-convex optimization landscapes that resemble needle-in-a-haystack surfaces, leading to entrapment in local minima. Contextualizing optimizers with human domain knowledge is a powerful approach to guide searches to localized fruitful regions. However, this approach is susceptible to human confirmation bias and it is also challenging for domain experts to keep track of the rapidly expanding scientific literature. Here, we propose the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for contextualizing Bayesian optimization (BO) via a hybrid optimization framework that intelligently and economically blends stochastic inference with domain knowledge-based insights from the LLM, which is used to suggest new, better-performing areas of the search space for exploration. Our method fosters user engagement by offering real-time commentary on the optimization progress, explaining the reasoning behind the search strategies. We validate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic benchmarks with up to 15 independent variables and demonstrate the ability of LLMs to reason in four real-world experimental tasks where context-aware suggestions boost optimization performance substantially.

This study introduces SLLMBO, an innovative framework leveraging large language models (LLMs) for hyperparameter optimization (HPO), incorporating dynamic search space adaptability, enhanced parameter space exploitation, and a novel LLM-tree-structured parzen estimator (LLM-TPE) sampler. By addressing limitations in recent fully LLM-based methods and traditional bayesian optimization (BO), SLLMBO achieves more robust optimization. This comprehensive benchmarking evaluates multiple LLMs, including GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-3.5, and Gemini-1.5-Flash, extending prior work and establishing SLLMBO as the first framework to benchmark a diverse set of LLMs for HPO. By integrating LLMs' established strengths in parameter initialization with the exploitation abilities demonstrated in this study, alongside TPE's exploration capabilities, the LLM-TPE sampler achieves a balanced exploration-exploitation trade-off, reduces API costs, and mitigates premature early stoppings for more effective parameter searches. Across 14 tabular tasks in classification and regression, the LLM-TPE sampler outperformed fully LLM-based methods and achieved superior results over BO methods in 9 tasks. Testing early stopping in budget-constrained scenarios demonstrated competitive performance, indicating that LLM-based methods generally benefit from extended iterations for optimal results. This work lays the foundation for future research exploring open-source LLMs, reproducibility of LLM results in HPO, and benchmarking SLLMBO on complex datasets, such as image classification, segmentation, and machine translation.

<jats:p>Software engineering (SE) now demands the navigation of vast configuration spaces, not only for software systems but also for the processes used to build them. Misconfigurations threaten performance, stability, and security. Worse, our ability to manually reason across large design spaces is limited. Hence we say (a) configurability is a liability without tool support and (b) as a priority, SE needs to explore better configuration tools.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Finding good configurations is a black art, requiring much experience. When that experience is scarce, “active learners” can build configuration models by labeling the most informative examples (so configurations can be generated using very little data).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Active learning can benefit from good initial guesses (known as “warm starts”). This article tries using Large Language Models (LLMs) for creating warm starts. However, LLM effectiveness diminishes in high-dimensional problems, where Bayesian methods like Gaussian Process Models perform best.</jats:p>
